transitivity: both — transitive (watch a movie), intransitive (just stand and watch)
gloss: To look at something for a period of time, following what happens.
examples: I *watch* the weather report before I leave for work.
We *watched* the fireworks from the roof.
He has been *watching* the same show for three hours.
contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person takes -es: watches, never watchs.

transitivity: both — transitive (observe the birds), intransitive (sit quietly and observe)
gloss: To watch something carefully in order to learn from it.
examples: Scientists *observe* the birds from a hidden blind.
The inspector *observed* that two windows were broken.
We have been *observing* the site since March.

gloss: To become aware of something by seeing, hearing or feeling it.
examples: Did you *notice* the new sign on the door?
Nobody *noticed* that I had left early.
I had never *noticed* the crack in the ceiling before.

gloss: To look at something, especially deliberately or from a particular place.
examples: Millions of people *view* the parade online every year.
We *viewed* three apartments on Saturday.
The exhibit can be *viewed* from the balcony.

gloss: To look at something very quickly and then look away.
examples: I *glance* at my phone far too often.
She *glanced* over her shoulder and kept walking.
He was *glancing* at the clock every few seconds.
contrast: Almost always needs a preposition: glance at the menu, glance over a letter — not glance the menu.

gloss: To look steadily at something for a long time, often without thinking.
examples: Tourists *gaze* up at the ceiling for a long time.
She *gazed* out the window and said nothing.
They stood *gazing* into the fire.
contrast: Needs a preposition: gaze at, gaze into, gaze out of.

gloss: To look hard at something that is difficult to see.
examples: I *peer* at the screen whenever the letters are small.
He *peered* through the fence to see the dog.
She was *peering* into the dark hallway.
contrast: Takes at, into or through. The noun peer (ровесник, коллега) is spelled the same but has nothing to do with looking.

gloss: To look at something quickly and secretly, often when you should not.
examples: Do not *peek* while I wrap the gift.
The kids *peeked* into the box anyway.
She caught me *peeking* at her notes.
contrast: Peek sounds exactly like peak (вершина) and pique (задеть). Only peek has to do with looking.

gloss: To see something for a very short moment and not clearly.
examples: From the train you *glimpse* the ocean for a second.
I *glimpsed* her face in the crowd and then lost her.
We had only *glimpsed* the house from the road.
contrast: The verb takes the object directly (glimpse the ship), but the noun needs of: catch a glimpse of the ship.

gloss: To see or notice something that is hard to see.
examples: Good editors *spot* mistakes fast.
I *spotted* him waiting by the gate.
She has *spotted* three eagles this month.
contrast: One short vowel plus one final consonant, so the t doubles: spotted, spotting.

gloss: To see something happen, especially a crime or an important event.
examples: Hundreds of people *witness* the ceremony every year.
Two neighbors *witnessed* the accident.
He has *witnessed* a lot of change in this town.

gloss: To look at something closely in order to judge its condition.
examples: Doctors *examine* the patient before surgery.
She *examined* the contract line by line.
The painting is being *examined* by an expert.

gloss: To look at something carefully to check that it is correct or safe.
examples: Officials *inspect* the kitchen twice a year.
He *inspected* the tires before the long drive.
They are *inspecting* the roof for storm damage.

gloss: To look over something quickly, usually to find one particular thing.
examples: I *scan* the headlines over breakfast.
She *scanned* the room for an empty seat.
He was *scanning* the list for his own name.
contrast: One short vowel plus one final consonant, so the n doubles: scanned, scanning.

gloss: To look over the whole of something in order to judge it.
examples: Researchers *survey* two thousand voters every month.
The pilot *surveyed* the damage from the air.
They are *surveying* the land before they build.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (sur-VAY); the noun on the first (SUR-vay). Vowel plus y keeps the y: surveys, surveyed.

transitivity: both — transitive (study the map), intransitive (she studies at night)
gloss: To look at something long and carefully in order to understand it.
examples: I *study* the map before every hike.
He *studied* her face for some sign of a reaction.
She has been *studying* the photographs all week.
contrast: Consonant plus y turns to i: studies, studied. But the -ing form keeps the y: studying.

gloss: To examine something very closely and critically.
examples: Auditors *scrutinize* every receipt.
The judge *scrutinized* the witness for a long moment.
His record has been *scrutinized* by the press.
contrast: American spelling is -ize; British writing uses scrutinise.

gloss: To look at someone in a long angry way.
examples: Some drivers *glare* when you take too long.
The teacher *glared* at the boy in the back row.
She just sat there *glaring* at her plate.
contrast: The angry sense takes at: glare at someone. The same verb also means to shine painfully: the sun glared off the snow.

gloss: To look with your eyes partly closed because of bright light or poor sight.
examples: I *squint* whenever I forget my glasses.
He *squinted* at the tiny print on the label.
She was *squinting* into the afternoon sun.

transitivity: both — transitive (blink your eyes), intransitive (the light blinked)
gloss: To shut and open your eyes quickly, or of a light, to flash on and off.
examples: Most people *blink* about fifteen times a minute.
The light *blinked* twice and went out.
He stared at me without *blinking*.

gloss: To close and open one eye quickly as a friendly or secret signal.
examples: Kids *wink* when they think they are being funny.
She *winked* at me across the table.
He kept *winking* to show that he was joking.
contrast: The person you signal takes at: wink at me, not wink me.

gloss: To look at someone or something with obvious interest or suspicion.
examples: Shoppers *eye* the new phones through the window.
The dog *eyed* my sandwich the whole time.
He was *eyeing* the last slice of pizza.
contrast: The -ing form keeps the e: eyeing. (Eying is possible but eyeing is the normal American spelling.)

transitivity: both — transitive (browse the catalog), intransitive (we are just browsing)
gloss: To look through things casually, without looking for anything in particular.
examples: I *browse* the shelves whenever I have time.
We *browsed* the market for an hour.
She was *browsing* online during the whole meeting.

transitivity: both — transitive (skim the article), intransitive (skim through a report)
gloss: To read something quickly to get the main idea.
examples: Editors *skim* the first page before reading closely.
I *skimmed* the article on the bus.
He was *skimming* the report, not really reading it.
contrast: The final m doubles: skimmed, skimming.

gloss: To watch something over time to see how it changes.
examples: Nurses *monitor* his heart rate all night.
We *monitored* the storm on radar.
The site is being *monitored* for fraud.
contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable, so the r does not double: monitored, monitoring.

gloss: To follow the movement or progress of someone or something.
examples: These apps *track* how far you walk.
Rangers *tracked* the bear for two days.
We have been *tracking* the package since Tuesday.

transitivity: both — transitive (spy a familiar face), intransitive (spy on the neighbors)
gloss: To watch someone secretly, or to catch sight of something suddenly.
examples: Neighbors *spy* on each other in that building.
She *spied* a familiar face in the crowd.
He was caught *spying* through the blinds.
contrast: Consonant plus y turns to i: spies, spied; the -ing form keeps the y: spying. Secret watching takes on: spy on someone.

gloss: To fail to notice or consider something.
examples: Tired eyes *overlook* small mistakes.
The bank *overlooked* two late payments.
One obvious clue had been *overlooked*.

gloss: To notice something but deliberately pay no attention to it.
examples: Please *ignore* the noise from upstairs.
He *ignored* three of my messages.
Her warning was *ignored* by everyone.

gloss: To notice something that is hard to see, hear or smell.
examples: Dogs *detect* smells that we cannot.
The alarm *detected* smoke at three in the morning.
No errors have been *detected* so far.

gloss: To become aware of something through the senses, or to understand it in a certain way.
examples: Cats *perceive* movement better than color.
We *perceived* a change in his tone at once.
The delay was *perceived* as rude.
contrast: Spelled -cei-, like receive and deceive: perceive, not percieve.

gloss: To feel that something is true without seeing direct proof of it.
examples: Animals *sense* a storm long before we do.
I *sensed* that something was wrong.
He had *sensed* the tension the moment he walked in.

gloss: To know someone or something because you have seen or heard them before.
examples: I *recognize* that voice.
She *recognized* him from an old photo.
The song was *recognized* instantly by the whole crowd.
contrast: American spelling is -ize; British writing uses recognise. The g is pronounced: REK-uhg-nyz.

gloss: To recognize someone or something and say exactly what or who it is.
examples: Witnesses *identify* the car by its bumper sticker.
The lab *identified* the sample in a day.
The bird has been *identified* as a young hawk.
contrast: Consonant plus y turns to i: identifies, identified; the -ing form keeps the y: identifying.

transitivity: both — transitive (distinguish the twins), intransitive (distinguish between the two)
gloss: To see or hear the difference between two similar things.
examples: Babies *distinguish* voices before they distinguish faces.
She *distinguished* the two samples by their smell alone.
I have trouble *distinguishing* blue from green.
contrast: Distinguish X from Y, or distinguish between X and Y.

gloss: To make out something that is faint or not obvious.
examples: Older readers *discern* the difference at once.
I *discerned* a note of doubt in her answer.
A clear pattern could be *discerned* in the data.

gloss: To find or learn about something for the first time.
examples: Kids *discover* something new every day.
We *discovered* a leak behind the washer.
It was later *discovered* that the file was missing.

gloss: To find exactly where something or someone is.
examples: The app can *locate* the nearest station for you.
Rescuers *located* the hikers before dark.
The office is *located* on the third floor.

gloss: To follow signs or clues back to the source of something.
examples: Detectives *trace* the call to a hotel downtown.
She *traced* the smell to a burnt wire.
The money has been *traced* to an offshore account.

gloss: To see something that was being searched for or watched for, usually at a distance.
examples: Sailors often *sight* whales off this coast.
A ranger *sighted* the missing dog near the river.
Three eagles were *sighted* here last spring.
contrast: Sight sounds exactly like site (место) and cite (цитировать). Only sight has to do with seeing.

gloss: To notice something and keep it in mind.
examples: Please *note* the change in the schedule.
He *noted* the time in the margin of the page.
As *noted* above, the deadline has moved.

transitivity: both — transitive (her face registered surprise), intransitive (the name did not register)
gloss: To notice something consciously, or for a feeling to show on someone's face.
examples: Loud noise does not *register* when you are that tired.
The joke *registered* a second too late.
I could see the news slowly *registering* on her face.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the r does not double: registered, registering.

gloss: To become aware of a fact that was true all along.
examples: Do you *realize* how late it is?
I *realized* my mistake halfway home.
He has finally *realized* that no one is coming.
contrast: American spelling is -ize; British writing uses realise.

gloss: To look at someone steadily, or to think of them in a particular way.
examples: Critics *regard* the film as a classic.
She *regarded* me for a moment without speaking.
The bridge is *regarded* as the best view in the city.
contrast: In the meaning to consider, it takes as: regard him as a friend, not regard him a friend.

gloss: To form a clear picture of something in your mind.
examples: Coaches tell players to *visualize* the shot first.
I *visualized* the room before I painted it.
She was *visualizing* the route in her head.
contrast: American spelling is -ize; British writing uses visualise.

gloss: To imagine how something looks.
examples: I can *picture* the house exactly.
He *pictured* himself on a beach somewhere.
Try *picturing* the room with white walls.

gloss: To come into sight, or to look a certain way to the people watching.
examples: Stars *appear* as soon as the sky darkens.
A crack *appeared* in the glass overnight.
He has *appeared* on that show twice.
contrast: In the meaning to seem, it is followed by an adjective or by to be: she appears tired, it appears to be broken.

gloss: To give the impression of being something.
examples: You *seem* tired today.
It *seemed* like a good idea at the time.
Nothing has *seemed* normal since Monday.
contrast: Sounds exactly like seam (шов). Seem is not used in the -ing form: say it seems fine, not it is seeming fine.

gloss: To put something where people can see it.
examples: Museums *display* only part of what they own.
The store *displayed* the new phones by the door.
The results are *displayed* on the screen.
contrast: Vowel plus y keeps the y: displays, displayed — not displaid.

gloss: To make something visible or known that was hidden.
examples: X-rays *reveal* what the eye cannot see.
She *revealed* the price at the very end.
The photo has *revealed* who else was in the room.

gloss: To uncover something, or to let something be reached by light, air or another influence.
examples: Photographers *expose* the film to light for a fraction of a second.
The storm *exposed* the roots of the old tree.
Children should not be *exposed* to that much noise.
contrast: What someone is brought into contact with takes to: exposed to sunlight, exposed to the language.

gloss: To keep something from being seen or known.
examples: Curtains *conceal* the wires behind the desk.
He *concealed* his surprise very well.
The camera was *concealed* inside a clock.

gloss: To remove a cover, or to find out something that was hidden.
examples: Journalists *uncover* stories that no one wants told.
We *uncovered* an old wood floor under the carpet.
New evidence has been *uncovered* this week.

transitivity: both — transitive (focus the lens), intransitive (focus on one thing)
gloss: To adjust your eyes or a lens until an image is sharp, or to give something your full attention.
examples: Try to *focus* on one sound at a time.
She *focused* the camera on his face.
He has been *focusing* on the wrong detail all morning.
contrast: American English keeps one s: focused, focusing. British writing often doubles it: focussed. Attention takes on: focus on the problem.

transitivity: both — transitive (tears blur your vision), intransitive (the edges blurred)
gloss: To make something unclear to see, or to become unclear.
examples: Tears *blur* everything for a minute.
The rain *blurred* the lights along the road.
The background has been deliberately *blurred*.
contrast: One short vowel plus one final consonant, so the r doubles: blurred, blurring.

gloss: To make something look or sound bigger than it really is.
examples: These lenses *magnify* the text four times.
The mirror *magnified* every flaw.
The sound was *magnified* by the empty hall.

transitivity: both — transitive (flash a light at someone), intransitive (the sign flashed)
gloss: To shine suddenly and briefly, or to make a light do that.
examples: Warning lights *flash* when the door is open.
Something *flashed* in the water near the boat.
The sign has been *flashing* all night.

gloss: To shine with an unsteady light that keeps going weak and strong.
examples: Old bulbs *flicker* before they die.
The candle *flickered* and went out.
The screen kept *flickering* during the call.

gloss: To shine softly, usually because a surface is clean or smooth.
examples: Clean windows *gleam* in the morning light.
His shoes *gleamed* under the stage lights.
A knife was *gleaming* on the counter.

gloss: To give off a steady, soft light without a flame.
examples: Embers *glow* long after the fire dies.
Her face *glowed* in the candlelight.
The screen was still *glowing* at midnight.

gloss: To shine with many small quick points of light.
examples: Fresh snow *sparkles* in the sun.
The water *sparkled* far below us.
Her eyes were *sparkling* with the news.

gloss: To shine with a hard, bright, broken light.
examples: Not everything that *glitters* is gold.
The dress *glittered* under the stage lights.
Broken glass was *glittering* on the pavement.

gloss: To make someone unable to see because of too much light, or to impress them greatly.
examples: Bright headlights *dazzle* oncoming drivers.
The show *dazzled* the whole crowd.
We were *dazzled* by the view from the top.

gloss: To light something up so it can be seen.
examples: Streetlights *illuminate* the path at night.
A single lamp *illuminated* the whole room.
The bridge is *illuminated* on holidays.
contrast: Double l, single m: illuminate, not iluminate.

gloss: To take away someone's sight, usually for a moment.
examples: Snow can *blind* you on a sunny day.
The flash *blinded* me for a second.
He was *blinded* by the low winter sun.

ru: звучать, казаться на слух; подавать сигнал
transitivity: both — intransitive (it sounds good), transitive (sound the alarm)
gloss: To give a particular impression when heard.
examples: Those two words *sound* the same to me.
Her voice *sounded* strange on the phone.
The alarm has been *sounding* for ten minutes.
contrast: An adjective follows directly: it sounds good. Before a noun use like: it sounds like a train.

transitivity: both — intransitive (the hall echoes), transitive (he echoed her words)
gloss: For a sound to come back off a surface and be heard again.
examples: These walls *echo* every footstep.
His question *echoed* down the hallway.
The room was *echoing* with laughter.
contrast: Ends in -o, so the third person adds -es: echoes, not echos.

gloss: To listen secretly to a conversation that is not meant for you.
examples: It is rude to *eavesdrop*.
She *eavesdropped* on the call from the hallway.
I caught him *eavesdropping* outside the door.
contrast: The final p doubles: eavesdropped, eavesdropping. It takes on: eavesdrop on a conversation.

gloss: To make a low continuous humming sound like an insect.
examples: Bees *buzz* around the porch all summer.
My phone *buzzed* twice during dinner.
The old lights were *buzzing* overhead.

transitivity: both — transitive (hum a tune), intransitive (the fridge hums)
gloss: To make a low steady sound, or to sing with your lips closed.
examples: Refrigerators *hum* at night when the house is quiet.
He *hummed* the tune all the way home.
The machine was *humming* softly in the corner.
contrast: The final m doubles: hummed, humming.

transitivity: both — intransitive (the clock chimed), transitive (chime the hour)
gloss: To make the clear ringing sound of a bell.
examples: Church bells *chime* at noon here.
The clock *chimed* six times.
We could hear bells *chiming* across the valley.

gloss: To make a long harsh sound, the way old wood or hinges do.
examples: Old stairs *creak* no matter how quietly you walk.
The door *creaked* open behind me.
The floorboards were *creaking* upstairs.
contrast: Creak sounds exactly like creek (ручей), but only creak is a sound.

gloss: To make a short high sound, like a mouse or a dry hinge.
examples: New shoes *squeak* on a gym floor.
The gate *squeaked* when I pushed it.
A mouse was *squeaking* somewhere behind the wall.

transitivity: both — intransitive (the window rattles), transitive (rattle the keys)
gloss: To make a series of short hard knocking sounds.
examples: Loose windows *rattle* in the wind.
The truck *rattled* over the old bridge.
Something was *rattling* around in the trunk.

transitivity: both — intransitive (leaves rustle), transitive (rustle the papers)
gloss: To make the soft dry sound of leaves or paper moving.
examples: Dry leaves *rustle* underfoot in October.
Her dress *rustled* as she stood up.
We heard something *rustling* in the bushes.
contrast: The t is silent: RUH-suhl, like castle and whistle.

transitivity: both — intransitive (the gravel crunched), transitive (crunch an apple)
gloss: To make a loud breaking sound when something hard is crushed or chewed.
examples: Fresh snow *crunches* under your boots.
He *crunched* an ice cube between his teeth.
The gravel was *crunching* behind us.

gloss: To make the hissing sound of food cooking in hot fat.
examples: Onions *sizzle* the moment they hit the pan.
The steak *sizzled* on the grill.
Bacon was *sizzling* when I came downstairs.

transitivity: both — intransitive (the timer beeped), transitive (beep the horn)
gloss: To make a short high electronic sound.
examples: The microwave *beeps* when it is done.
A truck *beeped* at us on the corner.
My watch kept *beeping* during the movie.

gloss: To make a very loud deep continuous sound.
examples: Jet engines *roar* on takeoff.
The crowd *roared* when he finally scored.
Traffic was *roaring* past the open window.

transitivity: both — intransitive (he whistled), transitive (whistle a tune)
gloss: To make a high clear sound by blowing air through your lips or a small opening.
examples: Some kettles *whistle* when the water boils.
He *whistled* for the dog.
She was *whistling* the same three notes all morning.
contrast: The t is silent: WIS-uhl.

gloss: To make a long s sound, like a snake or escaping steam.
examples: Cats *hiss* when they feel cornered.
The radiator *hissed* all night.
Steam was *hissing* out of the pipe.

gloss: To make someone unable to hear, usually for a short time.
examples: Sirens *deafen* you at close range.
The explosion *deafened* the workers nearby.
We were *deafened* by the music in that club.
contrast: The ea in deaf and deafen is /ɛ/ as in bed, not the /iː/ of leaf.

gloss: To make a sound quieter or less clear by covering it.
examples: Thick curtains *muffle* the street noise.
Snow *muffled* every sound in the yard.
His voice was *muffled* by the mask.

gloss: To make a sound or signal louder or stronger.
examples: Speakers *amplify* the sound for the back rows.
The empty hall *amplified* every footstep.
The signal is being *amplified* twice along the way.

transitivity: both — transitive (hush the baby), intransitive (the room hushed)
gloss: To become quiet, or to make someone be quiet.
examples: Parents *hush* their kids when the lights go down.
The crowd *hushed* as the curtain rose.
She was *hushing* the baby in the next room.

gloss: For a sound to go on ringing, or for an idea to strike people as true.
examples: Low notes *resonate* through the floor.
His speech *resonated* with young voters.
The sound was still *resonating* in my ears.
contrast: In the figurative sense it takes with: the story resonated with readers.

transitivity: both — intransitive (my phone vibrated), transitive (the motor vibrates the plate)
gloss: To shake with very small fast movements that you can feel or hear.
examples: Phones *vibrate* instead of ringing in meetings.
The whole table *vibrated* when the train passed.
My phone was *vibrating* in my pocket.

transitivity: both — transitive (sniff the milk), intransitive (the dog sniffed at my shoe)
gloss: To breathe in through the nose in order to smell something.
examples: Dogs *sniff* everything on a walk.
She *sniffed* the milk before pouring it.
He was *sniffing* the air as if something were burning.

transitivity: both — transitive (inhale the smoke), intransitive (inhale slowly)
gloss: To breathe air, smoke or a smell into your lungs.
examples: Try not to *inhale* the dust.
He *inhaled* deeply and started again.
She had *inhaled* smoke and needed oxygen.

gloss: To smell very strongly and unpleasantly.
examples: Those old sneakers *reek*.
The whole room *reeked* of fish.
His coat was *reeking* of smoke.
contrast: The source of the smell takes of: it reeks of gas, not it reeks gas.

gloss: To notice something by its smell, or to give something a pleasant smell.
examples: Hounds *scent* a fox from a mile away.
The bear *scented* us and ran.
These candles are *scented* with vanilla.
contrast: The c is silent, so scent sounds exactly like sent and cent.

transitivity: both — intransitive (it tastes sweet), transitive (taste the soup)
gloss: To notice the flavor of food or drink, or to have a particular flavor.
examples: These grapes *taste* sour.
I *tasted* the soup and added more salt.
Have you ever *tasted* real maple syrup?
contrast: An adjective follows directly: it tastes sweet. Before a noun use like: it tastes like lemon.

gloss: To enjoy a taste or an experience slowly and fully.
examples: Slow down and *savor* the first bite.
She *savored* every minute of the trip.
He sat there *savoring* his coffee.
contrast: American spelling is savor; British writing uses savour.

gloss: To try a small amount of something in order to judge it.
examples: Shoppers *sample* the cheese at the counter.
We *sampled* four kinds of local honey.
He was *sampling* everything on the table.

gloss: To move your tongue over something.
examples: Dogs *lick* your hand to say hello.
The cat *licked* the plate clean.
She was *licking* the spoon when I walked in.

transitivity: both — transitive (nibble a cracker), intransitive (nibble on a carrot)
gloss: To eat something in small bites.
examples: Mice *nibble* the corners of the box.
He *nibbled* a cracker and pushed the plate away.
She was *nibbling* on a carrot the whole time.
contrast: Eating slowly takes on or at: nibble on a cookie, nibble at her lunch.

transitivity: both — transitive (sip her tea), intransitive (sip at a glass)
gloss: To drink something slowly in very small amounts.
examples: Kids *sip* their drinks through straws.
She *sipped* her tea and said nothing.
He was *sipping* something hot from a paper cup.
contrast: The final p doubles: sipped, sipping.

gloss: To give food or drink a particular taste.
examples: Fresh herbs *flavor* the whole dish.
She *flavored* the cream with vanilla.
The rice was *flavored* with saffron.
contrast: American spelling is flavor; British writing uses flavour.

gloss: To add salt, pepper or spices to food to improve its taste.
examples: Good cooks *season* the meat before it goes in the pan.
I *seasoned* the soup a little too heavily.
The chicken had been *seasoned* overnight.

transitivity: both — transitive (press the button), intransitive (press against the door)
gloss: To push steadily on something with your hand or body.
examples: *Press* the button twice to start the machine.
He *pressed* his hand flat against the cold glass.
She was *pressing* the fabric down with both palms.

transitivity: both — transitive (rub your eyes), intransitive (the shoe rubs)
gloss: To move your hand or a cloth back and forth over a surface with pressure.
examples: I *rub* my eyes whenever I am tired.
He *rubbed* the stain with a wet cloth.
She was *rubbing* her sore shoulder.
contrast: The final b doubles: rubbed, rubbing.

transitivity: both — transitive (brush your coat), intransitive (brush against the wall)
gloss: To touch something lightly in passing.
examples: Low branches *brush* the roof of the bus.
Her sleeve *brushed* my arm as she passed.
Something soft was *brushing* against my leg.
contrast: A light accidental touch takes against: his coat brushed against mine.

gloss: To move your hand gently and repeatedly over a surface.
examples: Some cats let strangers *stroke* them.
She *stroked* the dog behind the ears.
He sat *stroking* his beard while he thought.

gloss: To touch something lightly several times with a flat hand.
examples: Coaches *pat* players on the back after a game.
He *patted* the seat next to him.
She was *patting* the dough into shape.
contrast: The final t doubles: patted, patting.

transitivity: both — transitive (tap the screen), intransitive (tap on the glass)
gloss: To hit something quickly and lightly, usually more than once.
examples: I *tap* the screen twice to zoom in.
Someone *tapped* me on the shoulder.
He kept *tapping* his pen against the desk.
contrast: The final p doubles: tapped, tapping. To touch a person it takes on: tap him on the arm.

transitivity: both — transitive (poke the cake), intransitive (poke at the fire)
gloss: To push a finger or a pointed object quickly into something.
examples: Do not *poke* the fire with your hand.
She *poked* the cake to see if it was done.
The kids were *poking* each other under the table.

gloss: To push someone or something gently, often to get attention.
examples: Friends *nudge* you when you have said too much.
She *nudged* me and pointed at the door.
He was *nudging* the box across the floor with his foot.

transitivity: both — transitive (pinch my arm), intransitive (these shoes pinch)
gloss: To squeeze something tightly between a finger and a thumb, or between two hard surfaces.
examples: New shoes always *pinch* at first.
He *pinched* my arm to wake me up.
The strap was *pinching* her shoulder.

transitivity: both — transitive (squeeze the lemon), intransitive (squeeze through a gap)
gloss: To press something firmly from two sides.
examples: *Squeeze* the lemon over the fish before serving.
She *squeezed* my hand and smiled.
He was *squeezing* the last of the toothpaste out.

gloss: To hold something tightly so it cannot slip.
examples: Good tires *grip* the road even in rain.
He *gripped* the rail with both hands.
She was *gripping* the steering wheel far too tightly.
contrast: The final p doubles: gripped, gripping.

gloss: To take firm hold of something with your hand, or to understand an idea.
examples: Babies *grasp* anything you put in their hand.
He *grasped* the rope and pulled himself up.
The idea is easily *grasped* once you see the diagram.

transitivity: both — transitive (clutch a bag), intransitive (clutch at a branch)
gloss: To hold something very tightly, often out of fear or need.
examples: Passengers *clutch* their bags on the subway.
She *clutched* the letter to her chest.
He was *clutching* a coffee in one hand and his keys in the other.
contrast: A desperate grab takes at: clutch at the rail.

ru: трогать руками, брать в руки; обращаться с
gloss: To touch or hold something with your hands.
examples: Please *handle* the glasses carefully.
He *handled* the vase as if it were made of paper.
These boxes have been *handled* roughly.

transitivity: both — transitive (tickle the baby), intransitive (this sweater tickles)
gloss: To touch someone lightly so that they laugh or twitch, or to cause a light itchy feeling.
examples: Wool sweaters *tickle* my neck.
He *tickled* the baby until she laughed.
My throat has been *tickling* all morning.

transitivity: both — intransitive (my arm itches), transitive (the wool itches me)
gloss: To feel an uncomfortable sensation on the skin that makes you want to scratch.
examples: Mosquito bites *itch* for days.
My eyes *itched* all through the spring.
The wool was *itching* against my skin.

transitivity: both — transitive (scratch your arm), intransitive (the dog scratched at the door)
gloss: To rub the skin with your nails, or to make a thin mark on a surface.
examples: Cats *scratch* the furniture when they are bored.
He *scratched* his head and said nothing.
She had *scratched* the side of the car backing out.

gloss: To touch or scrape a surface lightly while passing it.
examples: Low branches *graze* the roof of the bus.
The ball *grazed* his helmet and went wide.
She had *grazed* her knee on the pavement.
contrast: The same verb also means to eat grass: cows graze in the field.

transitivity: both — intransitive (fumble for the switch), transitive (he fumbled the ball)
gloss: To feel around for something clumsily, usually because you cannot see.
examples: Cold fingers *fumble* with small buttons.
He *fumbled* for the light switch in the dark.
She was *fumbling* with her keys at the door.
contrast: Searching by touch takes for or with: fumble for the switch, fumble with a zipper.

gloss: To feel a light prickling sensation on the skin.
examples: Cold air makes your cheeks *tingle*.
My fingers *tingled* after the snowball fight.
Her whole arm was *tingling* by then.

gloss: To feel a steady dull pain.
examples: My knees *ache* before it rains.
His back *ached* after the long drive.
She has been *aching* all over since the game.
contrast: The ch is pronounced /k/: AYK, not like church.

gloss: To take away feeling from a part of the body.
examples: Cold water will *numb* the pain for a while.
The dentist *numbed* the whole side of my mouth.
My feet were *numbed* by the cold.
contrast: The b is silent: NUM.

transitivity: both — transitive (probe the wound), intransitive (probe into his past)
gloss: To explore something by touch or by careful questioning.
examples: Doctors *probe* the wound for fragments.
Investigators *probed* the company's records for a year.
The whole area is being *probed* for leaks.
